name: Battle of Marengo
info: French forces under the First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte beat Michael von Melas's Austrian army near Alessandria in Piedmont on 14 June 1800 after a near defeat, and the Austrians left north-western Italy.

facts.place: On a plain east of Alessandria in Piedmont, northern Italy, between Marengo village, Castel Ceriolo and San Giuliano Vecchio, with the Fontanone stream between Marengo and the river Bormida
facts.sides: France under the First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte, with the Army of the Reserve officially commanded by Louis Alexandre Berthier: 22,000 men and 15 guns at first, with 6,000 more when Desaix arrived. Austria under General Michael von Melas: 30,000 men and 100 guns
facts.outcome: The Austrians, who had lost about half the forces they had committed, fell back into Alessandria. Within 24 hours Melas began negotiations that led to the Convention of Alessandria and the Austrian evacuation of north-western Italy west of the Ticino.

t: The Austrians attacked first and by mid-afternoon had broken the French centre, and the French were withdrawing when Louis Desaix arrived with fresh troops at around 5:30 pm and the battle turned.

Austrian losses were about half the forces they had committed: 15 colours, 40 guns, almost 8,000 prisoners and 6,500 dead or wounded, against French casualties of about 4,700 killed and wounded and 900 missing or captured.
Bonaparte's army bulletin and three 'Official Reports' during his rule made the battle seem more planned and more impressive than it was, though participants described an army often close to defeat.
dyk: Napoleon is said to have been told by Desaix, who was killed that evening, 'This battle is completely lost. However, there is time to win another.'
ev: Bonaparte leads his Army of the Reserve over the Alps into Italy
The French seize Milan and cut the main Austrian supply route along the south bank of the Po
Genoa surrenders to the Austrians, freeing a large number of them for operations against the French
The Austrians attack across the Bormida and break the French centre by early afternoon
Desaix's arrival and Kellermann's cavalry charge turn the battle, and the Austrians are routed
Melas begins negotiations that lead to the Convention of Alessandria
Napoleon holds a ceremony on the field to lay the founding stone of a pyramid

sections.background:
The battle was the last act of Bonaparte's Italian campaign of 1800. In mid-May he took his Army of the Reserve, officially commanded by Louis Alexandre Berthier, over the Alps almost before the passes were open, crossing on a mule, and threatened the lines of communication of the Austrian commander Michael von Melas in northern Italy. The French seized Milan on 2 June, followed by Pavia, Piacenza and Stradella, which cut the main Austrian supply route eastward along the south bank of the Po. Bonaparte hoped that Melas would be kept busy with the Siege of Genoa, held by André Masséna, but Genoa surrendered on 4 June and freed a large number of Austrians.

On 9 June Jean Lannes beat Feldmarschallleutnant Peter Ott at Montebello. Bonaparte became overconfident and convinced that Melas would not attack and that the Austrians were about to retreat. Melas had withdrawn most of his troops from their positions near Nice and Genoa to Alessandria on the main Turin-Mantua road. The Austrians planned to fight their way out eastward, but used a local double agent, usually known by his cover of François Toli, to make Bonaparte think they would march north, cross the Po and head for Milan.

Bonaparte knew that Ott had no way out from Alessandria but had no idea of Melas's position. Fearing that the Austrian general might escape, he spread his army in a wide net, sending Louis Desaix with Jean Boudet's division (6,000 men) south to Novi Ligure and La Poype's division (3,500 men) north on the other bank of the Po.
sections.forces:
The Austrians had 30,000 men and 100 guns, at first opposed by 22,000 French with 15 guns; the arrival of Desaix added 6,000 men to Bonaparte's army. The Austrian army had been worn down by the 1799 campaign, with casualties and disease reducing some regiments to 300 men, and only about 15% of the reinforcements sent from distant home bases reached the field army. Melas split it into three corps facing the Bormida in front of Alessandria: Ott in the north, with Gottesheim's advance guard and the divisions of Schellenberg and Vogelsang; O'Reilly's division in the south; and Melas himself in the centre, with the divisions of Hadik, Kaim, Morzin and Elsnitz.

The 36,000 French troops in Italy in 1799 had been in a desperate state, with supplies inadequate and discipline breaking down. For the Army of the Reserve Bonaparte first overhauled the supply system. Its core was 30,000 men, mostly from the Batavian Republic, who had been used under Brune to crush the rebellion in the Vendée, with veterans from the remains of the former Army of England. The new doctrine stressed the offensive, mobility and the bayonet over linear firepower.

The plain east of Alessandria was crossed by the meandering Bormida, over which the Austrians held a bridgehead, and was dotted with hamlets and farms. Marengo lay to the west, Castel Ceriolo to the north and San Giuliano Vecchio to the east, with the small Fontanone stream between Marengo and the Bormida. Victor's corps stood in and south of Marengo, Lannes's to the north-east, and Monnier's division and the Guard, the reserve, east of Castel Ceriolo.
sections.course:
The Austrians crossed the Bormida by two bridges into a narrow bend, and poor staff work meant the whole army had to file through a narrow bridgehead. The movement began about 6 am, the first shots came around 8 am and the attack was fully developed by 9 am. Melas's centre, about 18,000 men, was held at the Fontanone by Gardanne's division, and attacks by the divisions of Hadik and Kaim failed by 11 am, Hadik being killed. Ott's 7,500 men on the left took Castel Ceriolo around 11:30 am.

Bonaparte, 5 kilometres away, took until about 10 am to see that this was no diversion and was on the field by 11. Around 12:30 pm the Austrians bridged the Fontanone, and Victor, unable to hold, withdrew south-east, with Lannes mirroring him. By 2:30 pm the French were withdrawing and Austrian dragoons seized the Marengo farm. Bonaparte committed his main Guard battalion against Schellenberg's column, and after a 15-minute firefight around 4:00 pm it was surprised and destroyed by Frimont's cavalry. Melas, slightly wounded and 71, handed command to his chief of staff Anton von Zach and Kaim,.

Desaix reported to Bonaparte shortly before 5:00 pm with 6,000 men and 9 guns of Boudet's division. The 9th Light Infantry delayed the column for 30 minutes, Marmont's guns fired grapeshot, and Kellermann's heavy cavalry, about 400 men, charged Lattermann's grenadiers on the flank, which disintegrated. Desaix was shot from his horse and Zach and at least 2,000 of his men were taken. Murat and Kellermann routed the Liechtenstein Dragoons, and the Austrian infantry lost heart.
sections.aftermath:
The Austrians fell back into Alessandria, having lost about half the forces they had committed in 12 hours of fighting: 15 colours, 40 guns, almost 8,000 taken prisoner and 6,500 dead or wounded. French casualties were on the order of 4,700 killed and wounded and 900 missing or captured, but they kept the battlefield and the strategic initiative. Desaix's body was found among the slain. A last defence around Marengo village by Weidenfeld's second grenadier brigade, O'Reilly's returning cavalry and Frimont let the Austrian centre reach safety behind the Bormida as night fell, and Ott fought his way back to the bridgehead.

Bonaparte needed to leave for Paris urgently and the next morning sent Berthier to the Austrian headquarters. Within 24 hours Melas began the negotiations of the Convention of Alessandria, which led to the Austrians evacuating north-western Italy west of the Ticino and suspending military operations in Italy.

The outcome strengthened Bonaparte's position as First Consul after his coup of the previous November. Generals who had been hostile to him saw that his luck had not abandoned him, and he had done what Schérer, Joubert, Championnet and even Moreau had not, inflicting a decisive blow on the Coalition. He rejected offers from the Count of Provence, who had regarded the Consulate as a transition towards restoring the king. Moreau's victory at Hohenlinden in fact ended the war, and Bonaparte played it down.
sections.sources:
Accounts of the battle come largely from the commanders and officers on both sides and from what Bonaparte's government made of it. Melas wrote to Vienna that evening that Kellermann's charge had broken his soldiers, and Murat told Berthier that Kellermann's charge tipped the balance. In the army bulletin issued the next day, Napoleon set against it a charge by Bessières at the head of the Guard grenadiers. The battle was then mythologised in that bulletin and three increasingly glamourised 'Official Reports' during Bonaparte's reign, and tales were invented about the Guard and the 72nd demibrigade.

Berthier's Relation de la bataille de Marengo, published in 1804, presented the retreat as a calculated movement to give Desaix time to take position. Desaix's arrival was expected but not certain before the retreat, and the bulletin's claim that his force waited in reserve is false, since it arrived late. Marmont, Captain Coignet, Captain Gervais and General Thévenet all describe an army that was close to being beaten, with Coignet writing that they were 'all ready to start running at the earliest sign of danger'. Desaix's remark that the battle was lost rests only on a story.
sections.legacy:
Marengo is called a political victory that secured Bonaparte's grip on power after the coup, and a last-gasp victory in reality. Napoleon sought to ensure it would not be forgotten. On 5 May 1805 he and Joséphine presided over a ceremony on the field where General Chasseloup gave him the founding stone of a pyramid, part of a project for a 'city of Victories' whose boulevards, named after Italian battles, would converge on it. The project was abandoned in 1815 and the stones were recovered by peasants. A column erected in 1801 was removed and restored in 1922.

Several ships of the French Navy were named Marengo, and in 1802 a Marengo department was named in honour of the battle. Napoleon's mount at the battle was also called Marengo and carried him at Austerlitz, Jena-Auerstedt, Wagram and Waterloo. Marengo County in Alabama, first settled by Napoleonic refugees with their Vine and Olive Colony, was named for the battle, as were many settlements in Canada and the United States.

The dish chicken Marengo is named for the victory, and its recipe is generally credited to Dunan, chef to Napoleon's army in Italy, who made it in haste that evening. Puccini's Tosca of 1900, set in Rome a hundred years earlier, uses the battle: reports of an Austrian victory are corrected by news that Napoleon won, and Cavaradossi cries 'Vittoria!'. A museum of the battle, the Museo della Battaglia di Marengo, stands at Spinetta Marengo, and re-enactments are held every year.

summary: At Marengo on 14 June 1800 Napoleon Bonaparte's French army, nearly beaten by Melas's Austrians, was saved by Desaix's arrival and Kellermann's cavalry charge, and drove them back into Alessandria. Within 24 hours the Austrians began talks that took them out of north-western Italy.
notes: The article does not discuss its sources as such, so the sources section is built from the propaganda and eyewitness material it gives; it says nothing of archaeology or the main Austrian accounts.

Total losses: the lead says about 14,000 Austrians killed, wounded or captured; the body gives almost 8,000 prisoners and 6,500 dead or wounded. I gave the body's figures. The French figure of 4,700 plus 900 is 'on the order of'.
The article says 'Hadik's attack at 8 am' while the Austrians' movement was still deploying until 9 am, and that Gardanne held 'until about noon'; times are left as the article gives them.

Garbled or vandalised: 'Ott arrived from Montebello of 13 June in a war council'; the article first says Marengo fell about 2:00 pm and also that the farm was captured at 2:30 pm; 'Napoleon sought to counterbalance Kellermann's charge with Bessieres's' is quoted from the bulletin. 'Zach and at least 2,000 of his men were taken prisoners' sits oddly with Zach taking command from the wounded Melas. Left out: the coordinates of the headquarters, Chambarlhac 'lost his nerve and fled', and the article's judgement that Melas 'probably made a serious mistake'.
Left out for length: Pilatti's cavalry actions, Dampierre's 300-man detachment, O'Reilly's wasted time, the feigned detail of the Austrian plan to cross at Sale.
The dyk quote is given in the article as 'the story goes'. The ev entry 15 June 1800 is inferred from 'the next morning' and 'within 24 hours'; the article gives no date for the Convention.
